Four Canadians reached a four-way stop at the same time. Twenty minutes of polite waving later, they all knew each other's names and nobody had moved.

Someone bumped my cart at Costco and we both said sorry four times. We're basically cousins now.

The Tim's drive-thru line wraps around the building twice and every single person in it is calm. That might be the most Canadian sentence ever written.

A box of Timbits in the back seat lasts exactly one parking lot.

Driving past a Tim Hortons without stopping is possible. It has been done. Nobody in my family has ever witnessed it.

January mornings: start the car, scrape the windows, go inside to warm your hands, come back out, and the windows have frosted over again just to make a point.

Albertans keep a toque in the glovebox in July. Not because we expect snow. Because we've been fooled before.
Albertans wear shorts at plus 5 and parkas at plus 5. It depends which direction the season is coming from.
Alberta roads in March have five moods in one day: ice, slush, puddle, gravel and ice again.
Big Doug rode in a minor hockey minivan at 6 a.m. once. Three sleepy goalies used him as a pillow. He said "beauty" and closed his eyes too.

Every Alberta windshield has a rock chip and a story. "That one's from a gravel truck outside Red Deer, summer of 2021."

Every family car has a loonie in the cup holder for the grocery cart. It's been there so long it's technically a car part.

Big Doug can tell the temperature by the sound of the car door. "Crunch" is minus 20. "Crunch-crack" is minus 30. Silence means he's staying in.

Deerfoot at rush hour is where Calgary learns patience, one brake light at a time.

Big Doug has ended every sentence with "eh" for twenty years. Learners stop noticing around week two, eh.
In Jasper the elk lounge on front lawns like they pay property tax. Honestly, they might.

In Alberta you know winter's over when the pylons come out. You know winter's back when the pylons are still out.

Big Doug's chinook forecast: if his flannel's unbuttoned at noon in January, the chinook has arrived.
In Alberta, "the lake" is less of a place and more of a direction.
Every northern Alberta highway has one gas station that sells fuel, sandwiches, fishing gear and live bait at the same counter. It's the mall of the north.

Big Doug carries a Tim's card, a Canadian Tire card and a Costco card. He has no wallet. The flannel has a lot of pockets.
A Canada goose blocked the parking lot exit and honked at us. We don't speak goose, but we apologized anyway.
Tourists see a Mountie in red serge and get starstruck. Albertans see one and think, "That jacket would be great at minus 30."
Canadian horn etiquette: one tiny tap, then an apology wave, then thinking about it all evening.

Getting your learner's in Canada: you study for weeks, pass, and the first thing your parents say is "great, now you can drive us to Tim's."
Albertans will drive three hours for a good burger and call it "just down the road."
The prairie sky is so big the clouds look parked.
Big Doug rode the Banff Gondola once and spent the whole trip reaching for a handle that wasn't there.

Canadians don't brag about surviving winter. We just mention it casually, eleven times a day.
Every Albertan has a story about the coldest morning they ever started a car. It gets colder every time they tell it.

In Alberta you can tell how long someone's been awake by how much of their driveway is shovelled.

Alberta traffic report: slow on the Henday, busy on Deerfoot, and one Canada goose on the QE2 shoulder who refuses to be moved.
